newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan passes 97/98 budget, to tackle reforms.
newsitem.headline: Japan passes 97/98 budget, to tackle reforms.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto succeeded in pushing next fiscal year's state budget through parliament's key chamber on Wednesday, paving for way for the government to keep its promise to cut its bloated debt and tackle other reforms.

But some economists expressed scepticism over the government's promises, given its inability to cut legislators' pet projects out of the budget for 1997/98 -- the first year of promised fiscal reform.

"Looking at the way the budget was formed and was discussed through the parliament session, it's really hard to be optimistic about the various fiscal reforms the government promised to tackle," said Masaru Takagi, an economist at Fuji Research Institute Corp.

Hashimoto's ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and the two parties forming a loose alliance with it pushed the state budget through parliament's key Lower House, defying calls by opposition parties to revise the budget to cut spending.
The budget of 77.39 trillion yen ($639 billion) for the year from April 1 will now go to the Upper House, but Lower House approval virtually ensures its passage.
Defence spending for 1997/98 is allocated 4.95 trillion yen ($40.9 billion), up 2.1 percent from the 1996/97 budget.
Japan, the world's top aid donor, plans to increase funding for its official development assistance programme by 2.1 percent to 1.17 trillion yen ($9.6 billion).
General spending, the core of the budget, will total 43.81 trillion yen ($362 billion), up 1.5 percent from the amount earmarked in the original 1996/97 budget, the lowest growth since 1989/90.

The budget for 1997/98, which Hashimoto has said will be the first year of fiscal reform under a "Big Bang" deregulation plan, grew only 3.0 percent from last fiscal year's original budget. Hashimoto last November announced plans for Big Bang deregulation of Japan's financial markets by 2001.
The 1996/97 original budget was up 5.8 percent from the previous year.
Japan's fiscal deficit for calendar 1997 is seen at around 6.3 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP), one of the worst among major industrialised countries.

The budget was widely criticised for failing to drastically cut spending and for placing more of a burden on the public by ending special income tax cuts and raising the consumption tax to five percent from three percent from April.
The budget also hinted at the possibility of huge spending in the future by alloting funds to study the extension of existing lines for Shinkansen bullet trains.

Critics say attempts by ruling party politicians to have spending on bullet trains and other public works projects in their constituencies are making it difficult for the government to cut spending in public works and agricultural projects.

"Hashimoto has the enthusiasm to carry out reforms, but his leadership is not spreading to every corner of his party. He was unable to pin down demand from politicians with vested interests," Takagi said.

Hashimoto, stressing that the reforms will be carried out without further tax increases, has said the government plans to review its 10-year public works spending plan from 1995/96 totalling 630 trillion yen ($5.20 trillion).
The government has also promised to pass a law setting a numerical target for reducing state debt to three percent of annual gross domestic product by 2005.
It must also draft plans soon on how to deal with debts from the now defunct national railways amounting to over 28 trillion yen ($231 billion), starting from the 1998/99 budget. ($1=121 yen)
